title: We Were Completely WRONG About Megalodon

title_pattern.template: We Were Completely WRONG About [famous subject]
devices: myth-bust promise without saying which belief is wrong (curiosity gap)
subject is an already-famous noun with built-in search demand
title_pattern.notes: Title promises a correction; the video pays it off with several smaller corrections (not a great white ancestor, slender lemon-shark body instead of a stocky great white body, indirect extinction via whales and great whites) rather than one big reveal. Works as a channel-median performer (control), so this is the baseline format for the channel rather than an outlier.

thumbnail.composition: Full-bleed side profile of a giant shark filling ~85% of the frame, head pointing right with the open jaw lower right. A tiny scuba diver in a red suit is placed left of centre, against the shark's gill area. Two lines of text stacked across the top third.
thumbnail.text: Line 1: 'TOO BIG TO BE REAL' in bold red sans caps, small. Line 2: 'M E G A L O D O N' in very wide-tracked white/silver serif caps spanning the full width.
thumbnail.colours: Deep teal/navy underwater palette with dark vignette; white-grey shark skin; the only warm colours are the red diver and the red headline, so the eye goes diver -> headline -> shark eye/teeth.
thumbnail.subject_scale_contrast: Human diver about 1/12 of the shark's visible length; the shark is cropped by the frame edges, so it reads as bigger than the canvas. The scale contrast is the whole idea.
thumbnail.why_it_works: One clear idea (it's huge) shown in a single glance through a human scale reference; red accent on the human and the hook text; cinematic wide-tracked serif title reads as a 'documentary', not clickbait; the dark palette stands out from bright YouTube feeds. The thumbnail text adds a second claim ('too big to be real') instead of repeating the title.

hook.verbatim_0_10s: It was the early 1990s and a man named Vito Bertucci was searching the rivers of the southeastern United States for fossilized shark teeth.
hook.first_30s_summary: Cold-open true story: a named diver keeps finding palm-sized, serrated, triangular teeth in rivers where only small teeth should be: 'And they weren't rare. He kept finding them again and again.' The reveal at ~0:50 is 'That animal is known as the Megalodon.'
hook.device: Narrative cold open (named real person + era + place) that holds back the subject's name for ~50 s; a mystery object (giant teeth) builds intrigue before the reveal. No title card, no 'in this video'. Slow, calm documentary narration (~125 wpm in the first 12 s) over grainy, vintage-framed underwater footage, with a name lower-third at 0:03.
hook.visual_0_5s: Murky brown-green underwater riverbed footage inside a rounded-corner 'old film' frame on a dark grey border, then a portrait of Vito Bertucci with the lower-third 'VITO BERTUCCI (MEGALODON MAN)'.

beats.summary: Early 1990s, Vito Bertucci diving the southeastern US rivers for fossil shark teeth, where divers usually find small teeth from common prehistoric sharks.
He keeps finding unusually huge teeth (thick, triangular, serrated, palm-sized), again and again. They all belong to one kind of animal, bigger than any living shark.
Named: Megalodon. Problem: shark skeletons are cartilage, which doesn't fossilize, so there are no skeletons or outlines, only scattered teeth.

Bertucci collects hundreds of teeth and builds a full jaw from real specimens, using a great white jaw as the template. The jaw is big enough to stand inside: 'the scale was no longer theoretical. It was visible.'
Reframe: not 'did it exist?' but 'what kind of predator was this, how did it hunt, and how big was it?'
Black card with small disclaimer text saying some visuals are artistic interpretations.

The ocean as a place where size is invisible. A great white is about 6 m and already changes how people behave in the water. Megalodon is estimated at 15-20 m, and a 2025 vertebrae study puts the ceiling at ~24 m (80 ft). The numbers build on an animated size-comparison ruler.

The 'giant great white' image is wrong: at that scale metabolism, hunting and ecological role all change. With no living reference and no skeleton, the video lists open questions (speed, prey, ambush vs pursuit, what ocean could support it).

Why we know so little: whole-body cartilage (light, buoyant, flexible, an evolutionary win) rots, while teeth survive. About 40,000 teeth per lifetime are scattered worldwide. Size is inferred from tooth size, jaw curvature and bite marks on whale bones.

Bite force ~180,000 N vs great white ~18,000 N (10x), equal to three African elephants standing on one tooth. Serrated teeth and rib-cage fractures on whale fossils show it bit through whales, not around them.
Likely warm-blooded, needing ~100,000 kcal/day (50x a human). Failed hunts were costly, and this energy demand is 'the thread that eventually unravels the whole story'.

Not the great white's ancestor: 'about as closely related as a dog and a cat'. Otodontidae (bet on size and brute force) vs Lamnidae (smaller, faster, efficient), shown with a family tree. 'One of them had a longer shelf life.'
First appears ~23 Mya in warm, shallow, pre-baleen-whale oceans and is the apex predator over small toothed whales. Reigns ~13 My, compared with the human genus's ~3 My on a timeline graphic.

5-6 Mya slow tightening: climate cools, shallow seas retreat, coastal prey shrinks. Whales evolve baleen and 'skip the middleman' of the food chain (herring > cod > seal energy-loss graphic), then keep growing.
'Here's what gets interesting': the 2025 study matched its vertebrae to a lemon shark, not a great white. It was a long, slender cruiser at only 2-3 km/h with explosive bursts.

Handover: prey disappears or outgrows it while great white ancestors, suited to colder and deeper water, take the gap. The great white is an indirect cause: it was adapted to the ocean that was arriving.

'Is it still out there?' Steelman via the coelacanth (1938, South Africa, 'undiscovered for 66 million years'), then the rebuttal: the youngest teeth are 3.6 My old, modern whales carry no bite marks, and the coelacanth is low-energy while Megalodon was the opposite.

Its extinction lifted the size ceiling on baleen whales, and the blue whale (30 m, largest animal ever) could only exist afterwards. 'Their presence defines the ecosystem... but so does their absence.' Ends on a callback to the opening: a tooth on a seafloor 'waiting to be found'.
Dark seabed fades to a small 'Thank You!' text on black. No CTA voiceover.

pacing.avg_shot_length_note: 1153 s / ~218 shots from ffmpeg scene detection (threshold 0.3). Many changes are dissolves the detector misses, so the true visual-change interval is nearer 4-4.5 s. Infographic segments hold 6-16 s. Chapter breaks are marked by a 1-2 s fade through black, not a title card.
pacing.structure_note: Eight YouTube chapters of ~100-165 s each. Each chapter opens with a reframing line and ends with a forward-pointing line ('the thread that eventually unravels the whole story', 'one of them had a longer shelf life'). Music bed runs under the whole video with no sound-effect stings.

techniques_worth_copying: Cold open on a named real person, era and place, and hold back the subject's name for ~50 s; the mystery object (giant teeth) does the hooking.
Turn abstract scale into one visible artefact (a jaw you can stand inside) and say so: 'the scale was no longer theoretical. It was visible.'
Reusable size-comparison rig: cut-outs over a metres ruler with an animated scrubber and a label that steps up (20 ft -> 50-65 ft -> 80 ft), revisited in later chapters.
Pair every big number with a familiar reference: 10x a great white's bite, three elephants on one tooth, 100,000 kcal/day = 50 humans, 13 My vs 3 My of the human genus, 'dog and a cat' relatedness.
Lay out a mechanism step by step: decomposition sequence (soft tissue -> cartilage -> only teeth remain) shown as a locked-off seabed time-lapse.
An explicit foreshadow sentence plants the payoff ~7 minutes early (energy demand unravels the story).
A recurring 'here's what gets interesting / here's what most people get wrong' pivot every ~2-3 min to deliver the title's promised corrections.
Steelman the fan question ('Is it still out there?') with a real precedent (coelacanth) before debunking it with three evidence points.
Big-idea ending that widens the frame (its absence made the blue whale possible), then a circular callback to the opening tooth.
One consistent infographic language: dark teal/navy vignette background, white cut-outs, thin white callout lines, small all-caps labels, circular photo badges, timeline with a scrubber dot.
Chapters as plain descriptive labels in YouTube chapters only; on screen, a fade through black separates them.
Thumbnail: a tiny human beside a cropped giant, with red reserved for the human and the hook text.

code_only_remake_needs.summary: About 60% of the runtime is photoreal CGI/stock footage, which a code-only remake cannot match. The infographic language (~20% of runtime) maps cleanly to Remotion/SVG. The fix is to swap photoreal B-roll for a stylised vector ocean world and make the diagrams the hero instead of the interludes.
assets: SVG shark library: side-profile megalodon (stocky + slender variants), great white, mako, lemon shark, plus skeleton/x-ray overlay versions; tooth icon (serrated triangle); whale silhouettes (toothed early whale, humpback, blue whale with baleen highlight); herring, cod, seal; elephant; scuba diver; human-evolution figures

Parallax underwater scene: gradient water column (teal -> navy -> black), animated god rays, drifting particles/marine snow, caustics shader on the seabed, kelp and reef silhouettes, a surface line with waves for fin-at-surface shots
Procedural swim animation: body S-wave via SVG path morph or segmented bones, tail beat, slow cruise paths with camera follow
components: SizeRuler: cut-outs over a metres/feet ruler, animated scrubber, stepping label, auto-scaled silhouettes
Timeline: 'Years in Millions' axis with a scrubber dot and a big caps label (23 MILLION YEARS AGO, 3.6 MILLION YEARS AGO -> NOW)
Cladogram/FamilySplit: animated tree with node labels and cut-outs sliding to branches
Callout: circular magnifier badge + leader line onto part of a silhouette; label fade-in (CARTILAGE, BALEEN)
FoodChain: left-to-right cut-outs with arrows and shrinking energy bars, then a skip-arrow
StackAnalogy: objects dropping and stacking (elephants on a tooth)
DecaySequence: shark silhouette on seabed dissolving to skeleton, then to scattered teeth
MapOutline: glowing coastline/river stroke draw-on with location dots and circular photo badges
VintageFrame: rounded-corner inset with grain, vignette and sepia grade for 'historical' story beats (stand-in for archival photos: illustrated scenes or stylised portraits instead of real photos)
LowerThird name tag; DisclaimerCard; EndCard; fade-through-black chapter transition
code_only_remake_needs.audio_and_text: Calm documentary TTS (~140 wpm, slower ~125 wpm in the cold open), continuous ambient/cinematic music bed, no SFX stings, no burned-in captions in the original. A 19-minute runtime needs ~2,600 words of script and roughly 250 visual changes, so the remake needs a storyboard generator that cycles B-roll scenes every ~4-5 s with Ken Burns/camera drift so the stylised footage doesn't feel static.
code_only_remake_needs.gaps: Photoreal megalodon close-ups (eye, teeth, skin texture) and real-person archival photos have no code-only equivalent. Replace them with a stylised, high-contrast illustrated look and fictional or generic characters, not real people. The original also leans on stock nature footage, which needs code-drawn ocean scenes (aerial coast, storm, sunset) as gradient/shape compositions.
